[b]A Story from 1995 - Habara[/b]

[Spoiler=Prologue]
The sounds of droplets breaking the surface of cold water, echoes through the cave. Every man, not having found his inner peace yet, would meet insanity whilst listening to a silence, yet so loud. He does not. He was raised here.

It was 2002, the country already broken apart since several years, when the Naerim-Regime succesfully attempted to push forward into royal territory, to weaken their position in the highlands. The small village, going by the name of Habara, lays far off the next urban centre, New Daz. This is why they have been in the need of sustaining themselves for several years, ever since the crown stopped extending roads into small villages, through the NCI program. The people here dont live rich, although some would say their form of life brings all the freedom a man could wish for. The local farmers, together with the little hospital and primary school, keep the town running. Ordering any kind of goods will take up to multiple weeks of being delivered. 

The day the blue army troops, or liberation guards how the Naeris proclaim it, my father led us back into the caves. The whole towns population was gone, in a matter of days. When their officers arrived, they found nothing. It turned out it wasnt us, that they have seeked, but the position Habara lies in. A town, once forgettable, now prime hilltop for controlling the border roads. Not that any roads ran through Habara anymore, just the faded gravel that marked Naerims unfinished ambition. The soldiers marked their surprise with cigarettes and trash they left in the town square. They knocked on doors, found the school unlocked, the market empty, the bread shop still faintly scented with flour and yeast. But nothing else. They set up their base in the old assembly hall, strung banners, pointed parabolic microphones at the hills, and waited.

Down in the caves, we waited too. My fathers word was near-gospel, but even so, the first days were a struggle against disbelief. Some thought wed emerge to find it all a mistake, some accident, a single patrol or at worst a weeks inconvenience. It was only days later, when rationing became routine and the air thinned with body heat, that I watched the denial evaporate off the elders faces. The children, especially, caught on fast: the silence was loud, and every adults back was stooped in the same way, bent not by hunger alone, but fear. We learned new rituals. Each morning, my father or another chosen would walk the spine of the largest cave, counting us in low tones. Water from the stalactites was gathered in pans of battered aluminum. The hospital nurse, she was just called nurse, as if her life had erased all before that word, drew up lists of basic ailments and assigned children to carry tiny white tabs of aspirin, cut into halves and quarters. School continued, in a way, old textbooks illuminated by carefully rationed headlamps. It was strange. Truly.

The first week, a few brave men plotted escape. They studied the twists and passages, convinced there was a back exit toward the mines. None returned, but my father said nothing, only marked a line on the limestone with a piece of charcoal and never spoke their names again. For all we knew, they had found freedom or death or simply the wet, endless dark, which these caves gave away. More likely, it was the latter, but hope is as sticky as the sap of the old pines and will not wash out no matter how you try.
The idea of time began to dissolve. Days were measured by the slow consumption of food, by the dwindling of the nurses patience, by the clumping of childrens hair and the deepening shadows under eyes. Occasionally, above the ceiling, there would be a thunderclap of footfalls, soldiers running drills, or a truck groaning up the pass. The whole cave was stilled to listen. Sometimes we would hear gunfire, although they seemed rather distant. In the dark, my fathers face would be unreadable. And with our supply of wood and candled running out, it was always dark.
[/spoiler]

[Spoiler=Chapter I: A Blue Morning]
The convoy moved before sunrise.

We kept the lights off until the road bent out of the valley. After that, the drivers switched them on one by one, so they only glowed in dim beams. The engines might have just been the loudest thing I have ever heard. But that is just the feeling you get around these mountains to this hour. Six transport trucks, two armored carriers and a command jeep at the front.

I sat in the passenger seat of the jeep with a folded map on my knee. The driver, Corporal Eren, kept both hands on the wheel and said nothing. He knew better than to ask questions and show doubt during missions like this. Orders had come down late in the night from regional command. Secure Habara and establish permanent observation of the border pass, so we could report any signs of royalist movement. Habara had not been important two months ago. Now every officer in the Naerim command seemed to care about it.

The jeep climbed the last stretch of gravel slowly. The trucks behind us struggled with the incline. When we reached the ridge, I told Eren to stop. He braked without hesitation. I stepped out into the cold air and looked down toward the village. The sun was still below the horizon but the sky had started to brighten enough to see the layout clearly. Habara sat on a shallow plateau between to slopes. About forty buildings. Maybe less. A small square in the center. Primary school. Assembly hall. And a Market structure with a tin roof. No movement. 

I unfolded the map again even though I knew the ground already matched it. 

Sir, Eren said quietly, but not quietly enough, for my taste, from the drivers seat. I see it. Two Armored carriers rolled up behind us. The first one stopped beside the jeep. The hatch opened and Captain Selçuk climbed out. He adjusted the sling of his rifle and walked over. 

Theyre gone, he said. Yes. Selçuk looked down the slope again. Our scouts said there were civilians here last week., There were. He waited waited for more explanation. I didnt give one. The wind moved through the dry grass along the ridge. Down below, the village looked untouched. Like a ghost town. Doors closed. No vehicles. No voices. It was way too quiet. 

I folded the map and placed it back in my coat. Move the convoy down, I said. Selçuk nodded and signaled the armored crews. The vehicles started rolling down the path. Habara took fifteen minutes to reach from the ridge. The trucks spread into the open square and shut their engines off. Soldiers dismounted immediately and began moving through the streets in pairs. I walked toward the market building first. The door was unlocked. Inside, wooden shelves stood half full. Sacks of grain. Dried vegetables. A crate of glass jars. Selçuk entered behind me. Looks like they left in a hurry. No, I responded. He looked at me. They left in an organized way. I picked up a jar and set it back down. If people fled in panic they would leave doors open, animals would run loose, stoves would be left on and a house would burn down. That hadnt happened here. This place had been evacuated.

We stepped outside again. Across the square, soldiers were checking houses one by one. One of them called out that the school was empty. Another reported the same for the hospital building. Selçuk lit a cigarette. Maybe they heard we were coming. They heard something, I said. A lieutenant approached us at a jog. Sir. Yes? We found tracks leading toward the north slope. A lot of them. Recent? Two days. Maybe three. I nodded once. That meant they had left shortly before we arrived. Selçuk exhaled smoke and looked at the hills around the plateau. You think theyre hiding up there? Maybe. What do you want to do? I looked at the assembly hall across the square. Set up command there, I said. Get the radio team inside. I want microphones and observation gear on the north ridge before noon. Selçuk flicked the cigarette away. And the villagers? Theyre not the priority. He studied my face for a moment but didnt argue. That was one of the reasons he had been assigned to my detachment. You should stop smoking, I yelled after him as he was already gone, approaching the radio team. He responded with a middle finger, without paying me a glance.

The soldiers continued moving through Habara. Reports passed along the street in short sentences. One of the armored carriers parked beside the assembly hall. A sergeant stepped out carrying a crate of equipment. Sir, he said. Inside, I told him. Were turning this place into a observation post. He nodded and started issuing the order. 
I walked toward the edge of the plateau where the ground dropped toward the border road. From there the terrain made sense. The pass below was narrow. Any convoy moving through it could be seen from Habara long before reaching the ridge. Whoever controlled this village controlled the road. That was why command suddenly cared about it. But Ive known it all along.

Behind me I could hear soldiers setting up radio antennas and unpacking crates. The metallic sounds flew across the empty square. Selçuk came up beside me. Regional command wants a full report within the hour. Theyll get it. He looked down toward the pass. You think the royalists will try move through here? Eventually. And the civilians? They knew this place would become a military position. Selçuk crossed his arms. Smart people. Yes.

I turned back toward the village. The soldier had already raised the blue Naerim banner on the assembly hall roof. Habara now belonged to us. The villagers where somewhere in the hills and if they were organized enough to disappear this smoothly, someone had warned them. That meant someone else was watching the same roads we were.
 

The morning came with engine noise. 

I had slept two hours on a field cot inside the assembl hall. The building had once been the center of village meetings. I suppose so atleast. Now the wooden stage at the front held radio equipment and a long folding table covered with maps. Two antenna cables ran though the open window to a mast outside.

When I stepped out into the square the air was colder than the day before. Soldiers were already moving. One of the Toyota Landcruisers had started its engine to recharge the radio batteries. Two technicians were adjusting the parabolic microphone array on the roof of the school building across the square. Habara no longer looked abandoned.
Captain Selçuk stood near the jeep speaking with one of the signal operators. When he saw me he ended the conversation and walked over. You should get some more sleep Major. Im fine. Selçuk handed me a metal cup of coffee from the field kitchen. Radio check with command was clean this morning. They acknowledged your report. 

I drank the coffee slowly. It was strong and bitter. Whats their response? They want a permanent observation post here. Expected. Selçuk nodded. They also want patrols pushed into the hills. I looked toward the northern slope. The ridgeline above the village was still in shadow. How many teams? Two squads read now. I considered it for a moment. Send one east along the ridge. The other goes north. Selçuk gave a short nod and turned to signal one of the sergeants.

As he walked away I heard two younger soldiers talking near the truck. ...thats him, one of them said, noticeably quiet, but yet audible. The one from the border operation? Yeah. Demir. They stopped talking when they noticed I had looked in their direction. Rumors moved quickly in units like this. Especially when command attached someone new to the detachment. 

Selçuk came back after giving the orders. Theyre heading out in five minutes. Good. We watched the squads form up near the edge of the square. Twelve men total. Light gear and no vehicles. Theyll probably find nothing, Selçuk said. Probably. He glanced sideways at me. You know the men are curious. About what? About you. I didnt answer. Selçuk scratched his jaw. They heard stories. Someone in logistics told them you were intelligence before you came here. That was years ago. Still counts. I finished the coffee and handed the cup back to him.

The patrol teams started moving up the north road. I could still hear the sound of boots on gravel. One of the soldiers carried a portable radio folded along his pack. They disappeared between the trees within minutes. Selçuk watched them go. So did I. You ever been to this part of the country before? he asked. Yes. When? Long time ago. He waited. Back when they still controlled Marrin, I said. Selçuk raised an eyebrow. So before the war reached here. Yes. Doing what? Listening. 

That was the truth. 

Years ago I had spent most of my time in rooms with radios, radars and maps. Tracking movements along the frontier. Studying supply routes. Learning how officers in the royal command thought. I was one of the first contacts the Naerim Regime had within the ioyal inner reconnaissance circle. War eventually moved me out of those rooms.
Selçuk lit another cigarette. You know, he said, when headquarters told me Major Kemal Demir was joining my detachment I expected someone older. Disappointed? He smiled slightly. Just suprised. A Markades engine started behind us. The supply team was unloading more equipment crates.

Selçuk looked towards the hills again. You think the villagers are still nearby? Yes. Youre sure? They left too recently to travel far. He nodded slowly. So theyre watching us. Most likely. Selçuk exhaled smoke into the cold air. You ever wonder what they think when they look down here now? I followed his gaze toward the houses. The square was full of soldiers and blue-white banners hung down the assembly hall roof. Their village had become a military outpost in less than twenty-four hours. They most likely think were not leaving, I said. Selçuk didnt argue with that.

A signal operator ran across the square toward us. Sir. Yes. Observation team on the north ridge is picking up engine noise from the border road. What kind? Truck. They are not sure, guessing two. Selçuk looked at me. Royal convoy? Could be. I turned to ward the assembly hall. Lets go listen. Inside, the set up was already active. One of the technicians adjusted the microphone feed while another man wrote notes on a clipboard. Through the headphones the sound was faint but clear. Heavy engines. Moving slowly along the road below the ridge. Selçuk crossed his arms beside me. Supply trucks maybe. The technician increased the gain on the microphone. Voices. Distant. By far not clear enough to understand a word, but enough to know theyre here. Theyre closer than I thought. 

I studied the map spread across the table. The road below Habara curved through the pass before turning west toward the larger towns. If royal patrols were already moving through that route, the front line was shifting faster than command expected. Selçuk tapped the map with his finger. 

You think they know were here? 

No. But they will soon. 
[/spoiler]
